claim: During the first 2 postnatal weeks, mitochondrial motility decreases while the frequency of neuronal activity increases in the primary visual cortex of young mice.
source: During the first 2 postnatal weeks, mitochondrial motility decreases while the frequency of neuronal activity increases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Global calcium transients do not affect mitochondrial motility.
source: Global calcium transients do not affect mitochondrial motility.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the experiments.

claim: Individual synaptic transmission events precede local mitochondrial arrest.
source: However, individual synaptic transmission events precede local mitochondrial arrest.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the experiments.

claim: Pharmacological stimulation of synaptic vesicle release stops mitochondria.
source: Pharmacological stimulation of synaptic vesicle release, but not focal glutamate application alone, stops mitochondria, suggesting that an unidentified factor co-released with glutamate is required for mitochondrial arrest.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from pharmacological experiments.

claim: Focal glutamate application alone does not stop mitochondria.
source: Pharmacological stimulation of synaptic vesicle release, but not focal glutamate application alone, stops mitochondria, suggesting that an unidentified factor co-released with glutamate is required for mitochondrial arrest.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from pharmacological experiments.

claim: An unidentified factor co-released with glutamate is required for mitochondrial arrest.
source: Pharmacological stimulation of synaptic vesicle release, but not focal glutamate application alone, stops mitochondria, suggesting that an unidentified factor co-released with glutamate is required for mitochondrial arrest.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a speculation based on experimental findings.

claim: The developmental increase in synapse number and transmission frequency can contribute substantially to the age-dependent decrease of mitochondrial motility.
source: A computational model of synaptic transmission-mediated mitochondrial arrest shows that the developmental increase in synapse number and transmission frequency can contribute substantially to the age-dependent decrease of mitochondrial motility.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from computational modeling.

claim: Newborns can interact with their environment soon after birth, without any previous experience of sensory input.
source: Newborns can interact with their environment soon after birth, without any previous experience of sensory input.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Young networks are initially established by molecular guidance cues and refined by activity-driven synaptic plasticity.
source: Young networks are initially established by molecular guidance cues and refined by activity-driven synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Before the onset of sensory processing, developing neuronal networks generate neuronal activity spontaneously that strengthens well-targeted synapses and weakens others to prepare the brain for sensory processing.
source: Before the onset of sensory processing, developing neuronal networks generate neuronal activity spontaneously that strengthens well-targeted synapses and weakens others to prepare the brain for sensory processing. Later, learning adjusts synaptic circuits to the prevalent environmental conditions (Katz and Shatz, 1996; Sengpiel and Kind, 2002; Sanes and Yamagata, 2009; Kilb et al., 2011; Kirkby et al., 2013; Leighton and Lohmann, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Learning adjusts synaptic circuits to the prevalent environmental conditions.
source: Before the onset of sensory processing, developing neuronal networks generate neuronal activity spontaneously that strengthens well-targeted synapses and weakens others to prepare the brain for sensory processing. Later, learning adjusts synaptic circuits to the prevalent environmental conditions (Katz and Shatz, 1996; Sengpiel and Kind, 2002; Sanes and Yamagata, 2009; Kilb et al., 2011; Kirkby et al., 2013; Leighton and Lohmann, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The development of synapses and synaptic transmission are highly energy-demanding processes.
source: The development of synapses and synaptic transmission are highly energy-demanding processes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: A substantial amount of energy for synaptic development is supplied by mitochondria, the main energy providers in neurons.
source: A substantial amount of this energy is supplied by mitochondria, the main energy providers in neurons (Harris et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Neuronal mitochondria can be highly motile in intact tissue.
source: Imaging experiments showed that neuronal mitochondria can be highly motile in intact tissue (Misgeld et al., 2007; Plucińska and Misgeld, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Mitochondria are generated at the soma and transported to distal dendrites and axons via the microtubule network.
source: For example, mitochondria are generated at the soma and transported to distal dendrites and axons via the microtubule network (Sheng and Cai, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Mitochondrial motility allows for energy provision at high-energy-demanding sites, in particular, synapses.
source: This motility allows for energy provision at high-energy-demanding sites, in particular, synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from established knowledge.

claim: Defects in mitochondrial motility lead to impaired neurotransmission.
source: Defects in mitochondrial motility have been shown to lead to impaired neurotransmission, further linking mitochondrial motility and synaptic function (Sheng and Cai, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Experimentally enhancing neuronal activity stops mitochondria at synapses.
source: In addition, previous studies reported that experimentally enhancing neuronal activity (with high extracellular potassium, the voltage-gated sodium channel activator veratridine, glutamate, or electrical stimulation) stops mitochondria at synapses, whereas blocking action potential firing using tetrodotoxin (TTX) increases mitochondrial motility and reduces the number of stationary mitochondria at synapses (Rintoul et al., 2003; Li et al., 2004; Chang et al., 2006; MacAskill et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Blocking action potential firing using tetrodotoxin (TTX) increases mitochondrial motility and reduces the number of stationary mitochondria at synapses.
source: In addition, previous studies reported that experimentally enhancing neuronal activity (with high extracellular potassium, the voltage-gated sodium channel activator veratridine, glutamate, or electrical stimulation) stops mitochondria at synapses, whereas blocking action potential firing using tetrodotoxin (TTX) increases mitochondrial motility and reduces the number of stationary mitochondria at synapses (Rintoul et al., 2003; Li et al., 2004; Chang et al., 2006; MacAskill et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: MIRO1, a calcium-sensitive protein-linking mitochondria to the microtubule network, can mediate mitochondrial arrest in dendrites and axons.
source: MIRO1, a calcium-sensitive protein-linking mitochondria to the microtubule network, can mediate mitochondrial arrest in dendrites and axons (MacAskill et al., 2009; Wang and Schwarz, 2009): upon calcium binding, MIRO1 releases mitochondria from motor proteins (kinesins or dyneins), thus interrupting their motility.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Upon calcium binding, MIRO1 releases mitochondria from motor proteins (kinesins or dyneins), thus interrupting their motility.
source: MIRO1, a calcium-sensitive protein-linking mitochondria to the microtubule network, can mediate mitochondrial arrest in dendrites and axons (MacAskill et al., 2009; Wang and Schwarz, 2009): upon calcium binding, MIRO1 releases mitochondria from motor proteins (kinesins or dyneins), thus interrupting their motility.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Mitochondrial motility in neuronal dendrites is not affected by activity according to some evidence.
source: In contrast, other evidence suggests that mitochondrial motility in neuronal dendrites is not affected by activity (Beltran-Parrazal et al., 2006; Faits et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In retinal explants, neither spontaneously occurring nor stimulus-evoked activity affect mitochondrial motility.
source: In retinal explants, neither spontaneously occurring nor stimulus-evoked activity affect mitochondrial motility (Faits et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Mitochondrial motility remains high in a hyperactive retina with immature synapses.
source: Moreover, mitochondrial motility remains high in an hyperactive retina with immature synapses (Morrow et al., 2005; Tran et al., 2014; Faits et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: High mitochondrial motility may not be the consequence of low activity in immature tissue, but rather a characteristic of very young neurons.
source: These observations suggest that high mitochondrial motility may not be the consequence of low activity in immature tissue, but rather a characteristic of very young neurons (Faits et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a speculation based on cited evidence.

claim: Activity levels may co-vary with mitochondrial arrest rather than causing it.
source: Thus, activity levels may co-vary with mitochondrial arrest rather than causing it.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a speculation.

claim: In utero electroporation at embryonic day 16.5 was used to express the calcium indicator GCaMP6s and mitochondrial-DsRed in pyramidal neurons of layer II/III.
source: We used in utero electroporation at embryonic day 16.5 to express the calcium indicator GCaMP6s and mitochondrial-DsRed in pyramidal neurons of layer II/III (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological approach.

claim: There is an anti-correlation between the frequency of spontaneous global calcium transients and the percentage of moving mitochondria in awake animals.
source: Overall, we observed an anti-correlation between the frequency of spontaneous global calcium transients and the percentage of moving mitochondria in awake (unanesthetized) animals (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: In older animals (≥P8) activity levels were consistently higher and mitochondrial motility was low.
source: Upon closer inspection, it became clear that these parameters were linked systematically to the age of the animal: in older animals (≥P8) activity levels were consistently higher and mitochondrial motility was low (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2A-D.

claim: A similar relationship between neuronal activity, mitochondrial motility, and age was observed in anesthetized mice.
source: We observed a similar relationship between neuronal activity, mitochondrial motility, and age in anesthetized mice (0.8% isoflurane, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Application of TTX (2 µM) on the surface of the cortex completely abolished spontaneously occurring global calcium transients.
source: (E-F) Application of tetrodotoxin (TTX, 2 µM) on the surface of the cortex (n = 7 pups, 1625 mitochondria in 160 dendrites) completely abolished spontaneously occurring global calcium transients (paired t-test, p = 6*10–4) and increased the percentage of moving mitochondria (paired t-test, p = 0.035).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 2 caption and supported by the figure.

claim: Application of TTX (2 µM) on the surface of the cortex increased the percentage of moving mitochondria.
source: (E-F) Application of tetrodotoxin (TTX, 2 µM) on the surface of the cortex (n = 7 pups, 1625 mitochondria in 160 dendrites) completely abolished spontaneously occurring global calcium transients (paired t-test, p = 6*10–4) and increased the percentage of moving mitochondria (paired t-test, p = 0.035).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 2 caption and supported by the figure.

claim: Higher baseline frequency of spontaneous global calcium transients was correlated with a larger effect of TTX on the percentage of moving mitochondria.
source: (G) Higher baseline frequency of spontaneous global calcium transients was correlated with a larger effect of TTX on the percentage of moving mitochondria (n = 7 pups, Pearson correlation, r = 0.85, p = 0.015).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 2 caption and supported by the figure.

claim: The percentage of moving mitochondria did not change significantly between the 2 minutes before and after spontaneously occurring global calcium transients in awake animals.
source: (H-I): Mean mitochondrial motility time-locked to the onset of single global calcium transients. The percentage of moving mitochondria did not change significantly between the 2 minutes before and after spontaneously occurring global calcium transients in awake animals (n = 136 transients, paired t-test, p = 0.33).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 2 caption and supported by the figure.

claim: Natural patterns of neuronal activity efficiently constrain mitochondrial motility.
source: Furthermore, the effect of TTX on mitochondrial motility was highly proportional to the frequency of baseline activity (r2 = 0.81; Figure 2G), suggesting that natural patterns of neuronal activity efficiently constrain mitochondrial motility.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Spontaneous global calcium transients did not precede a change in mitochondrial motility.
source: We found that spontaneous global calcium transients did not precede a change in mitochondrial motility (Figure 2H–I) or mitochondrial speed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by figures.

claim: Spontaneous global calcium transients did not precede a change in mitochondrial speed.
source: We found that spontaneous global calcium transients did not precede a change in mitochondrial motility (Figure 2H–I) or mitochondrial speed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by figures.

claim: Synaptic transmission, rather than postsynaptic action potential firing, might regulate mitochondrial motility.
source: We therefore speculated that synaptic transmission, rather than postsynaptic action potential firing, might regulate mitochondrial motility.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a speculation based on the findings.

claim: Slices obtained from older animals showed a trend toward higher spontaneous activity levels.
source: Slices obtained from older animals showed a trend toward higher spontaneous activity levels (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B) and significantly lower mitochondrial motility than slices obtained from younger animals (Figure 3B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by figures.

claim: Slices obtained from older animals showed significantly lower mitochondrial motility than slices obtained from younger animals.
source: Slices obtained from older animals showed a trend toward higher spontaneous activity levels (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B) and significantly lower mitochondrial motility than slices obtained from younger animals (Figure 3B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by figures.

claim: In slice cultures, spontaneous global calcium transients did not precede changes in mitochondrial motility.
source: As in vivo, spontaneous global calcium transients did not precede changes in mitochondrial motility (Figure 3C–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D) or speed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by figures.

claim: In slice cultures, spontaneous global calcium transients did not precede changes in mitochondrial speed.
source: As in vivo, spontaneous global calcium transients did not precede changes in mitochondrial motility (Figure 3C–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D) or speed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by figures.

claim: Visual cortex layer II/III neurons frequently showed spontaneous calcium transients in spines representing synaptic transmission events at excitatory synapses.
source: In slice cultures, visual cortex layer II/III neurons frequently showed spontaneous calcium transients in spines representing synaptic transmission events at excitatory synapses, as shown previously in the developing visual cortex and hippocampus (Kleindienst et al., 2011; Winnubst et al., 2015; Niculescu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: In nine cells (P5 + 3–7 DIV), 71 out of 157 spines (45%) showed spontaneous synaptic calcium transients.
source: In nine cells (P5 + 3–7 DIV), we identified 157 spines of which 71 (45%) showed spontaneous synaptic calcium transients (376 transients).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a quantitative observation.

claim: Mitochondria typically passed by inactive synapses.
source: We observed that mitochondria typically passed by inactive synapses (Figure 3E), but frequently halted when they reached a synapse that had just been active (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3E.

claim: Mitochondria frequently halted when they reached a synapse that had just been active.
source: We observed that mitochondria typically passed by inactive synapses (Figure 3E), but frequently halted when they reached a synapse that had just been active (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3F.

claim: The percentage of stopping mitochondria increased significantly after a synaptic calcium transient.
source: When we compared the percentage of stopping mitochondria during a 120 s interval before a single synaptic calcium transient occurred with an interval of the same duration after that calcium transient, we found that the percentage of stopping mitochondria increased significantly after the transient (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3I.

claim: The observed effect size of mitochondrial arrest at active synapses was above the 95 percentile of the randomized effect size distribution.
source: We found that the observed effect size was above the 95 percentile of the randomized effect size distribution (Figure 3J) demonstrating that this effect was unlikely to be observed by chance.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3J.

claim: Mitochondrial arrest was most prevalent within distances of up to 5 µm around a synapse and for intervals of 80–120 s after the synaptic event.
source: Next, we quantified the effect size for different distances from the synapse and different time intervals after a synaptic calcium transient and found that mitochondrial arrest was most prevalent within distances of up to 5 µm around a synapse and for intervals of 80–120 s after the synaptic event (Figure 3K and L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3K and L.

claim: On average, synaptic activity was associated with an interruption of mitochondrial movement for about 1 min (68 s).
source: On average, synaptic activity was associated with an interruption of mitochondrial movement for about 1 min (68 s; Figure 3M).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3M.

claim: One-third of the stopping mitochondria were still immobile at the end of a recording.
source: However, this number underestimated the duration of arrest, since one-third of the stopping mitochondria were still immobile at the end of a recording (mean 131 s at a recording duration of 350 s) preventing an exact estimate of the time point when they started moving again.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a quantitative observation.

claim: Spontaneous synaptic transmission can capture moving mitochondria in postsynaptic dendrites.
source: Together, our observations at individual synapses suggested that spontaneous synaptic transmission can capture moving mitochondria in postsynaptic dendrites.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: An increase of extracellular potassium to 50 mM decreased mitochondrial motility by approximately 50%.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Li et al., 2004; MacAskill et al., 2009; Faits et al., 2016), we found that an increase of extracellular potassium to 50 mM decreased mitochondrial motility by approximately 50% (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4A and B.

claim: Long-lasting depolarization arrests mitochondria.
source: This result demonstrated that long-lasting depolarization arrests mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Global calcium transients, which are most likely the consequence of depolarization-induced opening of voltage-gated calcium channels, suggest that depolarization alone is insufficient to stop mitochondria.
source: However, our finding that global calcium transients, which are most likely the consequence of depolarization-induced opening of voltage-gated calcium channels, suggest that depolarization alone is insufficient to stop mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: At the concentration used (1 nM), latrotoxin specifically triggers synaptic vesicle release through activation of its receptors latrophilin and neurexin that are located at presynaptic terminals.
source: Nevertheless, at the concentration used here (1 nM), latrotoxin specifically triggers synaptic vesicle release through activation of its receptors latrophilin and neurexin that are located at presynaptic terminals (Valtorta et al., 1984; Matteoli et al., 1988; Südhof, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: After application of latrotoxin to the bath, the intracellular calcium concentration increased within a few minutes and mitochondrial motility was either entirely suppressed or largely inhibited.
source: After application of latrotoxin to the bath, the intracellular calcium concentration increased within a few minutes and mitochondrial motility was either entirely suppressed or largely inhibited (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3C-E (likely Figure 4C-E based on context).

claim: Mitochondrial motility recovered only partly after around 1 hr, whereas calcium levels returned to baseline levels within 15–20 min.
source: Mitochondrial motility recovered only partly after around 1 hr, whereas calcium levels returned to baseline levels within 15–20 min.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a quantitative observation.

claim: Single synaptic transmission events have the capacity to stop mitochondria for 1 to a few minutes.
source: These experiments indicated that single synaptic transmission events have the capacity to stop mitochondria for 1 to a few minutes and that massive synaptic activation interrupts mitochondrial motility almost entirely for periods of tens of minutes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Massive synaptic activation interrupts mitochondrial motility almost entirely for periods of tens of minutes.
source: These experiments indicated that single synaptic transmission events have the capacity to stop mitochondria for 1 to a few minutes and that massive synaptic activation interrupts mitochondrial motility almost entirely for periods of tens of minutes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Focal glutamate delivery triggered calcium increases in the dendrite extending 7–59 µm (27 ± 14 µm; mean ± standard deviation).
source: Focal glutamate delivery triggered calcium increases in the dendrite extending 7–59 µm (27 ± 14 µm; mean ± standard deviation).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a quantitative observation.

claim: Mitochondrial motility was slightly, but not significantly, reduced after glutamate puffs.
source: We found that mitochondrial motility was slightly, but not significantly, reduced after glutamate puffs (Figure 4F and G), demonstrating that glutamate is not sufficient to cause vesicle release-mediated mitochondrial arrest.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4F and G.

claim: Glutamate is not sufficient to cause vesicle release-mediated mitochondrial arrest.
source: We found that mitochondrial motility was slightly, but not significantly, reduced after glutamate puffs (Figure 4F and G), demonstrating that glutamate is not sufficient to cause vesicle release-mediated mitochondrial arrest.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Synaptic vesicle release interrupts mitochondrial transport locally.
source: While the factor that mediates mitochondrial arrest remains unknown, our experiments showed that synaptic vesicle release interrupts mitochondrial transport locally.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Synaptic density increases dramatically in the cortex during the second postnatal week.
source: Since synaptic density (De Felipe et al., 1997) as well as network activity (Rochefort et al., 2009) and thus synaptic vesicle release increase dramatically in the cortex during the second postnatal week, we hypothesized that the temporary recruitment of mitochondria to synapses by spontaneous synaptic activity could contribute to the overall decrease in mitochondrial motility we observed during in vivo development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Network activity increases dramatically in the cortex during the second postnatal week.
source: Since synaptic density (De Felipe et al., 1997) as well as network activity (Rochefort et al., 2009) and thus synaptic vesicle release increase dramatically in the cortex during the second postnatal week, we hypothesized that the temporary recruitment of mitochondria to synapses by spontaneous synaptic activity could contribute to the overall decrease in mitochondrial motility we observed during in vivo development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Synaptic vesicle release increases dramatically in the cortex during the second postnatal week.
source: Since synaptic density (De Felipe et al., 1997) as well as network activity (Rochefort et al., 2009) and thus synaptic vesicle release increase dramatically in the cortex during the second postnatal week, we hypothesized that the temporary recruitment of mitochondria to synapses by spontaneous synaptic activity could contribute to the overall decrease in mitochondrial motility we observed during in vivo development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from cited evidence.

claim: The temporary recruitment of mitochondria to synapses by spontaneous synaptic activity could contribute to the overall decrease in mitochondrial motility observed during in vivo development.
source: Since synaptic density (De Felipe et al., 1997) as well as network activity (Rochefort et al., 2009) and thus synaptic vesicle release increase dramatically in the cortex during the second postnatal week, we hypothesized that the temporary recruitment of mitochondria to synapses by spontaneous synaptic activity could contribute to the overall decrease in mitochondrial motility we observed during in vivo development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a hypothesis.

claim: A mean density of 36 active synapses per 100 µm dendrite was found in visual cortex layer II/III pyramidal neurons at the end of the second postnatal week (P10–15).
source: In our previous in vivo study, we found a mean density of 36 active synapses per 100 µm dendrite in visual cortex layer II/III pyramidal neurons at the end of the second postnatal week (P10–15) and transmission occurred 0.6 times per minute at each synapse (Winnubst et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Transmission occurred 0.6 times per minute at each synapse in visual cortex layer II/III pyramidal neurons at the end of the second postnatal week.
source: In our previous in vivo study, we found a mean density of 36 active synapses per 100 µm dendrite in visual cortex layer II/III pyramidal neurons at the end of the second postnatal week (P10–15) and transmission occurred 0.6 times per minute at each synapse (Winnubst et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: A 100 µm dendrite receives synaptic inputs at a frequency of approximately 0.36 Hz at the end of the second postnatal week.
source: We estimated, therefore, that a 100 µm dendrite receives synaptic inputs at a frequency of approximately 0.36 Hz.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from cited data.

claim: Anatomical studies showed a 5–10 times increase of synaptic density in the developing sensory cortex between P5 and P11.
source: Anatomical studies showed a 5–10 times increase of synaptic density in the developing sensory cortex between P5 and P11 (De Felipe et al., 1997) and we found here that neuronal activity doubled from the first to the second postnatal week (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Neuronal activity doubled from the first to the second postnatal week.
source: Anatomical studies showed a 5–10 times increase of synaptic density in the developing sensory cortex between P5 and P11 (De Felipe et al., 1997) and we found here that neuronal activity doubled from the first to the second postnatal week (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: Synaptic input frequencies should be about 0.02–0.04 Hz at P5.
source: Assuming that release probabilities do not change dramatically during this period, synaptic input frequencies should be about 0.02–0.04 Hz at P5.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from cited data and assumptions.

claim: There is a 16 times increase in synaptic transmission events in dendrites of V1 layer II/III pyramidal cells from P8 to P13.
source: Similarly, we find in in vivo patch-clamp and calcium imaging experiments a 16 times increase in synaptic transmission events in dendrites of V1 layer II/III pyramidal cells from P8 to P13 (AH Leighton et al. 2021, in preparation).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to unpublished work.

claim: An increase in synaptic input frequency from P5 to P12 would reduce mitochondrial motility by 30–60% depending on the actual arrest times at synapses.
source: As Figure 5C shows, an increase in synaptic input frequency in this range would reduce mitochondrial motility by 30–60% depending on the actual arrest times at synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5C.

claim: A 70% decrease in mitochondrial motility was observed between the first and second postnatal week.
source: Since we observed a 70% decrease in mitochondrial motility between the first and second postnatal week, our model showed that temporary immobilization of mitochondrial motility through synaptic signaling can mediate a large proportion of this effect.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a quantitative observation.

claim: Temporary immobilization of mitochondrial motility through synaptic signaling can mediate a large proportion of the developmental decrease in mitochondrial motility.
source: Since we observed a 70% decrease in mitochondrial motility between the first and second postnatal week, our model showed that temporary immobilization of mitochondrial motility through synaptic signaling can mediate a large proportion of this effect.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the model.

claim: Synaptic vesicle release, but not action potential firing, plays a primary role in the reduction of mitochondrial motility with dendrite maturation.
source: Together, our data suggest a primary role of synaptic vesicle release, but not action potential firing, in the reduction of mitochondrial motility with dendrite maturation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Mitochondrial motility and positioning are fundamental for axon and dendrite development and synaptic plasticity.
source: Mitochondrial motility and positioning are fundamental for axon and dendrite development and synaptic plasticity (Courchet et al., 2013; Kimura and Murakami, 2014; Fukumitsu et al., 2015; López-Doménech et al., 2016; Vaccaro et al., 2017; Divakaruni et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Mitochondrial dynamics are affected in many neurological disorders.
source: Moreover, mitochondrial dynamics are affected in many neurological disorders (Chen and Chan, 2009; Deheshi et al., 2013; Misgeld and Schwarz, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Regulation of mitochondrial motility is important for neuronal function.
source: Thus, regulation of mitochondrial motility is important for neuronal function; however, to what degree neuronal activity determines mitochondrial motility in intact neuronal circuits has been unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as established knowledge.

claim: Dendritic mitochondria in retinal explants and axonal mitochondria in the visual cortex show similar decreases in motility during development.
source: Given that dendritic mitochondria in retinal explants and axonal mitochondria in the visual cortex show similar decreases in motility (Chang and Reynolds, 2006; Faits et al., 2016; Lewis et al., 2016; Smit-Rigter et al., 2016), our results confirm a general progression towards more stationary mitochondria in intact tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The results confirm a general progression towards more stationary mitochondria in intact tissue during development.
source: Given that dendritic mitochondria in retinal explants and axonal mitochondria in the visual cortex show similar decreases in motility (Chang and Reynolds, 2006; Faits et al., 2016; Lewis et al., 2016; Smit-Rigter et al., 2016), our results confirm a general progression towards more stationary mitochondria in intact tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the data and cited evidence.

claim: Synaptic activation, but not action potential firing, arrests mitochondrial motility.
source: That synaptic activation, but not action potential firing, arrests mitochondrial motility is in fact consistent with the majority of observations of activity-dependent regulation of mitochondrial motility in hippocampal and cortical neurons (Li et al., 2004; Chang et al., 2006; MacAskill et al., 2009; Wang and Schwarz, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Activity manipulations affect both action potential firing and synaptic transmission, and it is possible that synaptic release changes, but not firing alone, altered mitochondrial motility in previous studies.
source: Since activity manipulations, such as depolarizing neurons by increasing extracellular potassium, blocking action potential firing with TTX, and electric field stimulation affect both action potential firing and synaptic transmission, it is possible that synaptic release changes, but not firing alone, altered mitochondrial motility in these studies.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation based on the findings.

claim: A local factor, either by itself or together with glutamate, mediates mitochondrial arrest.
source: Our observations that pharmacological activation of synaptic vesicle release arrests mitochondria, but that neither spontaneous global activation nor focal glutamate application stops moving mitochondria, suggest that a local factor, either by itself or together with glutamate, mediates mitochondrial arrest.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation based on the findings.

claim: ATP is a possible candidate for the local factor that mediates mitochondrial arrest.
source: A possible candidate is ATP: it is present in synaptic vesicles and released simultaneously with glutamate at excitatory cortical synapses (Khakh, 2001; Burnstock, 2007; Lalo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation with supporting citations.

claim: ATP is present in synaptic vesicles and released simultaneously with glutamate at excitatory cortical synapses.
source: A possible candidate is ATP: it is present in synaptic vesicles and released simultaneously with glutamate at excitatory cortical synapses (Khakh, 2001; Burnstock, 2007; Lalo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: ATP receptors of the P2X and P2Y families are expressed in cortical pyramidal cell dendrites.
source: ATP receptors of the P2X and P2Y families are expressed in cortical pyramidal cell dendrites (Guzman and Gerevich, 2016), trigger postsynaptic depolarizations (Pankratov et al., 2002) and calcium increases (Lalo et al., 1998; Lalo and Kostyuk, 1998), activate CaMKII (Pougnet et al., 2014) and mediate synaptic plasticity (Pankratov et al., 2009; Lalo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: ATP receptors trigger postsynaptic depolarizations.
